_about: Field terms for F209, same shape as papers/glossary.json.

crescograph.definition: an instrument built by J. C. Bose from about 1917 that magnifies the lengthening of a plant shoot with compound levers, or in a later version a magnetic needle and a light beam, and records it as a trace
crescograph.excludes: modern optical or electronic growth sensors, which touch the plant far less

dendrometer.definition: a gauge that records the size of a tree stem, here an electronic sensor reading the stem radius many times a day
dendrometer.excludes: any direct count of new wood cells; the gauge records size, which also changes with the water held in the stem

zero-growth.definition: the rule, due to Zweifel and colleagues, that a stem is counted as growing only while it exceeds its own previous maximum radius, with every reading below that maximum treated as water deficit
zero-growth.excludes: the linear-growth alternative, in which growth is assumed to continue through periods of shrinkage

dead-band.definition: the range of input movement to which a mechanism gives no output, from slack or friction in its joints; here 0.05 micrometres at the specimen
dead-band.excludes: random noise, which moves the output both ways

hygroscopic.definition: the change in size of a material as it takes up water vapour from the air; plant tissue, wood and gut strings all lengthen or swell this way with no living process involved
hygroscopic.excludes: growth, which adds new cells or enlarges living ones, and thermal expansion

vpd.definition: the difference between the water vapour pressure of saturated air at the current temperature and the vapour pressure the air has; a measure of how strongly the air draws water from a plant
vpd.excludes: relative humidity, which is a ratio and does not scale with drying demand across temperatures

false-alarm.definition: a detection reported when the event did not happen; here a growth stop flagged on a simulated stem that never stops growing
false-alarm.excludes: an early flag on a stem that does stop later, which is counted apart

inverse-crime.definition: testing a reconstruction or detection method on synthetic data produced by the same model the method assumes, which makes the method look better than it is on real data
inverse-crime.excludes: tests on data from a different or richer model, and tests on measurements

misfit.definition: a difference between the process that made the data and the model the analysis assumes; here a slower water memory, an unmodelled rain store and a noisier humidity record
misfit.excludes: measurement noise alone, which the matched scenarios also contain
